--- title: "Residuals, Least Squares, and Model Evaluation" author: "Prof. Eric Friedlander" footer: "[🔗 MATH 2025 - Fall 2026 - Schedule](https://ericfriedlander.github.io/math2025-fa26/schedule)" logo: "../images/logo.png" format: revealjs: theme: slides.scss multiplex: false transition: fade slide-number: false incremental: false chalkboard: true html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" execute: freeze: auto echo: true cache: false knitr: opts_chunk: R.options: width: 200 bibliography: references.bib --- ## Topics - Define residuals, and connect them to the idea of variation in $Y$. - Understand how the least squares method chooses a regression line. - Partition variation into model and error (ANOVA), and use it to compute $R^2$ and RMSE. ## Last time {.smaller} ::: {.incremental style="font-size: 0.9em"} - Regression works with a categorical predictor $X$, just like a quantitative one. - R recodes a $K$-level categorical variable into $K - 1$ **indicator (dummy) variables**, dropping the **reference level**. - The intercept is the mean of the response at the reference level; each slope is the difference in means from that level. - We started playing with the **Coffee Truck** to generate our own data. ::: ## Computational set up ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # load packages library(tidyverse) # for data wrangling and visualization library(ggformula) # for plotting using formulas library(broom) # for formatting model output library(scales) # for pretty axis labels library(knitr) # for pretty tables library(kableExtra) # also for pretty tables library(patchwork) # arrange plots library(yardstick) # for R^2 and RMSE # Spotify Dataset spotify <- read_csv("../data/spotify-popular.csv") # set default theme and larger font size for ggplot2 ggplot2::theme_set(ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = 20)) ``` ::: ## Quick Data Cleaning ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} spotify <- spotify |> mutate(duration_min = duration_ms / 60000) ``` ::: ::: question - What is this code doing? - Why might I be doing it? ::: ## The regression model, revisited {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} spotify_fit <- lm(danceability ~ duration_min, data = spotify) tidy(spotify_fit, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95) |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| conf.low| conf.high| |:------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:|--------:|---------:| |(Intercept) | 0.781| 0.028| 28.351| 0.000| 0.727| 0.835| |duration_min | -0.024| 0.008| -3.151| 0.002| -0.039| -0.009| ::: ::: - There is strong statistical evidence that there is a linear relationship between the duration of a song and its danceability. - We are 95% confident that as the length of a song increases by one minute the danceability will decrease by between 0.009 and 0.039 units. # Residuals ## From points to a line {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06-slr-fitting-eval_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: question For any one song, how far off is the line from the actual data point? ::: ## Residuals {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06-slr-fitting-eval_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: $$\text{residual} = \text{observed} - \text{predicted} = y_i - \hat{y}_i = e_i$$ ::: {.fragment} - A **positive** residual: the point is *above* the line (model underpredicted). - A **negative** residual: the point is *below* the line (model overpredicted). ::: # Partitioning Variability ## Let's think about variation :::{.incremental} - DATA = MODEL + ERROR - $\substack{\text{Variation} \\ \text{in Y}} = \substack{\text{Variation explained} \\ \text{by model}} + \substack{\text{Variation not explained} \\ \text{by model}}$ - Every point's residual is a leftover piece of variation the model didn't explain. ::: ::: question If we drew *any* other line through the cloud of points, would the residuals get bigger or smaller? Is there a "best" line? ::: # Least squares ## Choosing values for $\hat{\beta}_1$ and $\hat{\beta}_0$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](06-slr-fitting-eval_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: question Which of these three lines does the "best" job? How would you decide? ::: ## The least squares method {.smaller} ::: incremental - We need a rule for picking *the* line, not just *a* line. - **Least squares method**: choose $\hat{\beta}_0$ and $\hat{\beta}_1$ to minimize the sum of squared residuals $$ \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 $$ - Why square the residuals instead of just adding them up? + Positive and negative residuals would cancel out. + Squaring also penalizes large misses more than small ones. ::: ## Properties of least squares regression {.smaller} ::: incremental - Passes through the center of mass point, the coordinates corresponding to average $X$ and average $Y$: $\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}$ - Slope has same sign as the correlation coefficient: $\hat{\beta}_1 = r \frac{s_Y}{s_X}$ + $r$: correlation coefficient + $s_Y, s_X$: sample standard deviations of $X$ and $Y$ - Sum of the residuals is zero: $\sum_{i = 1}^n e_i \approx 0$ + Intuition: Residuals are "balanced" - The residuals and $X$ values are uncorrelated ::: ## Estimating the slope, by hand {.smaller} $$\large{\hat{\beta}_1 = r \frac{s_Y}{s_X}}$$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} s_x <- sd(spotify$duration_min) s_y <- sd(spotify$danceability) r <- cor(spotify$duration_min, spotify$danceability) s_x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.7524002 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} s_y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.1314275 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} r ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.1387227 ``` ::: ::: ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} b1 <- r * s_y / s_x b1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.02423176 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} Compare to `lm()`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} coef(spotify_fit)["duration_min"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` duration_min -0.02423176 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Estimating the intercept, by hand {.smaller} $$\large{\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}}$$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x_bar <- mean(spotify$duration_min) y_bar <- mean(spotify$danceability) b0 <- y_bar - b1 * x_bar b0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.7809197 ``` ::: ::: Compare to `lm()`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} coef(spotify_fit)["(Intercept)"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) 0.7809197 ``` ::: :::
::: small [Click here](https://introregression.netlify.app/98-appendix) for details on deriving the equations for slope and intercept, which is easy if you know multivariate calculus. ::: # Partitioning Variability (ANOVA) ## Splitting up the residual {.smaller} :::{.incremental} - $y_i - \bar{y} = (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y}) + (y_i-\hat{y}_i)$ - Square and sum: $\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2 = \sum(\hat{y} - \bar{y})^2 + \sum(y-\hat{y})^2$ - $\substack{\text{Sum of squares} \\ \text{Total}} = \substack{\text{Sum of squares} \\ \text{model}} + \substack{\text{Sum of squares} \\ \text{error}}$ - $SSTotal = SSModel + SSE$ - $SST = SSM + SSE$ - ANOVA: Analysis of Variance ::: ## ANOVA in R ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} spotify_fit |> anova() |> tidy() |> kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | df| sumsq| meansq| statistic| p.value| |:------------|---:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:| |duration_min | 1| 0.1685294| 0.1685294| 9.928516| 0.0017237| |Residuals | 506| 8.5889829| 0.0169743| NA| NA| ::: ::: ## Recall: Correlation Coefficient - The **correlation coefficient**, $r$, is a number between -1 and +1 that measures how strong the linear relationship between two variables $x$ and $y$ is. $$ r = \frac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2}} = \frac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{s_xs_y} $$ ## Two statistics: $R^2$ {.smaller} ::: incremental - **R-squared**, $R^2$, **Coefficient of Determination**: Percentage of variability in the outcome explained by the regression model (in the context of SLR, the predictor) $$ R^2 = Cor(y, \hat{y})^2 $$ - Also called **PRE (Percent Reduction in Error)** because: $$ R^2 = \frac{SSModel}{SSTotal} $$ ::: ## $R^2$ ::: incremental - Ranges between 0 (terrible predictor) and 1 (perfect predictor) - Has no units - Calculate with `rsq()` from `yardstick` package using the augmented data: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} spotify_aug <- augment(spotify_fit) rsq(spotify_aug, truth = danceability, estimate = .fitted) |> kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |.metric |.estimator | .estimate| |:-------|:----------|---------:| |rsq |standard | 0.019244| ::: ::: ::: ## Interpreting $R^2$ {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: poll 🗳️ **Discussion** ::: midi The $R^2$ of the model for `danceability` from `duration_min` is 1.9%. Which of the following is the correct interpretation of this value? ::: 1. `duration_min` correctly predicts 1.9% of `danceability`. 2. 1.9% of the variability in `danceability` can be explained by `duration_min`. 3. 1.9% of the variability in `duration_min` can be explained by `danceability`. 4. 1.9% of the time `danceability` can be predicted by `duration_min`. ::: ## Activity ::: appex In groups, at the board, design a simulation-based procedure for producing a p-value for the following hypothesis test. - $H_0: R^2 = 0$ - $H_A: R^2 \neq 0$ ::: ## RMSE {.smaller} ::: incremental - **Root mean square error, RMSE**: A measure of the average error (average difference between observed and predicted values of the outcome) $$ RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n}} $$ + Sometimes people just care about numerator (SSE) or version without the square-root (MSE) + Sometimes the denominator may have $n-1$ instead - Ranges between 0 (perfect predictor) and infinity (terrible predictor) - Same units as the response variable - Interpretation (kind of): how much does my model miss by, on average. ::: ## RMSE in R ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rmse(spotify_aug, truth = danceability, estimate = .fitted) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 .metric .estimator .estimate 1 rmse standard 0.130 ``` ::: ::: # Back to the Coffee Truck ## Comparing models with $R^2$ {.smaller} Recall Jo's coffee truck: **Business District**, **Lunch**, **Weather = Constant** the whole time. Today, each group will generate **three** data sets with the [Coffee Truck game](https://www.stat2games.sites.grinnell.edu/games/coffeetruck.html): | Data set | What varies | What's held fixed | |:--:|:--|:--| | `music` | Music (No Music / Hip Hop / Alternative) | Price = \$3 | | `price` | Price (\$2 / \$3 / \$4 / \$5) | Music = No Music | | `both` | Music **and** Price | — | ::: appex 📋 [AE 06 - Comparing Models with the Coffee Truck](../ae/ae-06-coffee-truck-eval.qmd) ::: Complete Exercises 1-3. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## A data cleaning wrinkle {.smaller} The game exports `Price` as **text**, e.g. `"$3"`, not a number: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Price | |:-----| |$2 | |$3 | |$4 | |$5 | ::: ::: ::: question Why does this matter for fitting `lm(Sales ~ Price)`? What do we need to do first? ::: . . . Same fix as before: strip the `$` and convert. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} price <- price |> mutate(Price = str_replace(Price, "\\$", "")) |> mutate(Price = as.numeric(Price)) ``` ::: Complete Exercises 4-9. ## The comparison {.smaller} You'll fit `Sales ~ Music` on **`music`**, and both `Sales ~ Music` and `Sales ~ Price` on **`both`**. ::: question Music's effect on `Sales` didn't change between `music` and `both`. So why might $R^2$ for `Sales ~ Music` be so different in these two data sets? ::: . . . - In `music`, price is fixed — all the leftover variability in `Sales` is either explained by music or is pure noise. - In `both`, price is also bouncing around. That extra variability inflates **SST**, so the *same* music effect now explains a *smaller share* of a *bigger* pie. Complete Exercises 10-12. If time permits, complete Exercise 13. ## Using the word "Good" - There is no such thing as a "Good" $R^2$ or, especially, RMSE without context. - Whether your model is a "Good" model depends on many things: + What are you using your model for? + How good are other models? + **What else was varying in the data you fit it to?** ## Recap {.smaller} - A **residual** is the leftover gap between an observed value and the model's prediction: $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$. - The **least squares method** picks $\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1$ to minimize $\sum e_i^2$. - Can decompose total variation (SST) into variation explained by the model (SSM) and leftover variation (SSE). - Two metrics for evaluating and comparing models: + $R^2$: What proportion of the variation in the response variable is explained by the model? + $RMSE$: How far does my model miss by, on average? - $R^2$ depends on the data it was fit to, not just the true relationship — so it can't be compared across data sets that vary different things.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
